strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across nine datasets spanning three distinct task types (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is broader than most competing event-based works.

The proposed Event Cloud representation with explicit polarity handling and chronological ordering addresses a genuine limitation of prior Point Cloud-based event methods (loss of polarity, treating time as pseudo-spatial dimension).

Strong efficiency results: substantially lower MACs and higher throughput/FPS than frame-based and voxel-based competitors while achieving comparable or superior accuracy, which is practically relevant for event-camera applications requiring low power and low latency.

The frequency-domain module (Spatial-FA/Temporal-FA) is reasonably well motivated by complexity analysis (O(D^2) vs O(D log D)) and grounded in established frequency-domain learning literature (FFC, GFNet, SpectFormer).
Ablation studies (Tab. 7, Tab. 8) probe the contribution of individual components (G&S design, TFA module, polarity, event number scaling) and support the design choices to some degree.
Preprocessing time comparison (Tab. 3) is a useful practical consideration often overlooked in event-representation papers.
weaknesses: No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple-run statistics are reported for any table, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 16% or 26% improvements) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run variance, especially since some datasets (e.g., Daily DVS with only 731 test samples) are small.

Several key architectural design choices (e.g., choice of scaling factor α in D-FPS, filter initialization V, number of loops=3, specific hidden dimensions) are stated as fixed settings without justification or sensitivity analysis, limiting insight into robustness of the design.

The claim 'FECNet pioneers leveraging Event Cloud representation' is somewhat overstated given that reference [48] (Wang et al., WACV'19) is explicitly cited as already using 'Space-time event clouds' terminology; the novelty claim needs clearer differentiation from this prior work beyond stating it ignores polarity.

The paper does not provide code (the abstract states 'code is available at' but no link is given), and implementation details (e.g., exact network configs per dataset beyond what's in text, training seeds) are insufficiently detailed for full reproducibility.
Comparison baselines in some tables mix pretrained-on-ImageNet and non-pretrained models inconsistently, and it is unclear whether FECNet itself uses any pretraining, complicating fair comparison.

The efficiency claims (MACs, FPS) are only benchmarked on a single dataset (DVS128 Gesture, Tab. 5) and single hardware platform (RTX 4090); given diverse dataset scales (T ranges from 1024 to 8192), broader efficiency benchmarking across datasets would strengthen the efficiency claims.

Writing contains several grammatical errors and awkward phrasing throughout (e.g., 'FECNet pioneer leverages', 'Experimemt' typo repeated in table captions, 'Abaltion' typo), which detracts from clarity and suggests insufficient proofreading.

The description of the CES (Coordinates Evolution Strategy) and the overall interaction between coordinate updates and feature updates is dense and somewhat hard to follow without a clearer worked example, reducing reproducibility for readers not already familiar with point-based hierarchical networks.

Limitations of the approach (e.g., potential sensitivity to noise in raw events since Event Cloud is 'nearest to raw output' without denoising, generalization to unseen event densities, or failure cases) are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated efficiency/fidelity trade-off in event representations (frame/voxel vs point cloud), and the proposed Event Cloud representation that retains polarity while avoiding costly frame/voxel conversion is a sensible and relatively underexplored direction.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning nine datasets and three distinct tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation) is commendable in scope compared to many event-representation papers that focus on a single task.

The efficiency numbers (MACs, FPS, parameter counts) reported in Tables 5 and 6 are compelling if accurate, showing large reductions relative to frame- and voxel-based competitors while matching or exceeding their accuracy.

The ablation studies (Table 7, Table 8) attempt to isolate the contribution of individual components (G&S design, Temporal-FA, polarity, event count scaling) which supports some of the internal design claims.

The idea of applying global frequency-domain filtering to long, irregularly sampled event sequences to avoid LSTM/attention overhead is a reasonable and moderately novel adaptation of existing frequency-domain learning techniques (FFC, GFNet) to the event-cloud setting.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is seriously undermined: the abstract promises code availability but the link is blank/missing, and no other reproducibility artifacts (hyperparameter files, released checkpoints, or detailed architecture per dataset beyond the group-count table) are provided.

No error bars, standard deviations, or multiple-seed runs are reported anywhere in the tables; given that several accuracy gaps versus baselines are small (e.g., N-CARS, N-Caltech101, ASL-DVS), the significance of the reported improvements cannot be assessed.

The theoretical justification for the Spatial-FA module (claiming Hadamard product in frequency domain is 'mathematically analogous... with the same performance' to a learned convolution) is asserted rather than proven or empirically verified via a controlled comparison; the complexity reduction argument (factor of 60/20x) is a rough back-of-envelope calculation not tied to measured wall-clock or verified MACs breakdown per module.

Overclaiming language throughout ('pioneer', 'ground-breaking results', 'amazing results') is not well supported by the modest and sometimes inconsistent margins over prior SOTA (e.g., only 0.1-0.3 points gain on several classification datasets), which weakens the credibility of the significance claims.

Comparisons across tasks may not be fully controlled: e.g., in human pose estimation, competing methods use different Point Cloud variants (RPC) with distinct backbones/sizes, and in the pretrained-vs-non-pretrained classification tables, it is unclear whether FECNet was ever tested with a pretraining protocol comparable to the strongest frame-based baselines.

The manuscript has numerous typographical and formatting errors (e.g., 'Experimemt', 'Abaltion', 'moudle', 'specturm', inconsistent capitalization of table captions), suggesting insufficient proofreading, which raises concern about the overall care taken in preparing and possibly verifying the technical content.

No explicit limitations section or discussion of failure cases; the paper does not discuss scenarios where Event Cloud/frequency-domain modeling might underperform (e.g., extremely sparse or extremely dense event streams, sensitivity to the choice of scaling factor α, or sensitivity of D-FPS/EF-KNN hyperparameters).

The claim that frequency-domain filters are 'global' and thus superior at capturing long/short-term dependencies is not substantiated by any frequency-spectrum visualization or interpretability analysis; the claimed advantage over LSTM/attention (Table 8) is based on only one dataset and one sliding window setting, which is a narrow basis for such a general claim.

Statistical/qualitative failure analysis (e.g., confusion matrices, qualitative pose estimation visualizations, or class-wise breakdowns) is entirely absent, limiting insight into where and why the method succeeds or fails relative to baselines.

strengths: Introduces a new 'Event Cloud' representation (2S-1T-1P) that retains polarity information and avoids costly frame/voxel conversion, addressing a genuine gap between Point Cloud and frame/voxel methods.
Novel Event-based Grouping & Sampling module (D-FPS, EF-KNN, CES) that explicitly differentiates spatial, temporal, and polarity dimensions rather than treating time as a quasi-spatial coordinate.

Frequency-domain (Spatial-FA and Temporal-FA) modules are a sensible and well-motivated way to reduce MACs while capturing long-range temporal dependencies in long event sequences, with reasonable complexity analysis (O(D log D) vs O(D^2)).

Extensive empirical validation across nine datasets and three distinct tasks (classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), with consistent SOTA or near-SOTA accuracy alongside substantially lower MACs/parameters and higher throughput than frame- and voxel-based baselines (e.g., Tables 2, 4, 5, 6).
Reasonably thorough ablations (module ablation in Table 7, event-number scaling with LSTM comparison in Table 8) that support the specific design choices (polarity, Temporal-FA, event-based G&S).
weaknesses: No standard deviations, multiple runs, or statistical significance testing are reported for any of the results; given some margins (e.g., N-Caltech101, N-Cars) are narrow, it's unclear if gains are robust to run-to-run variance.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'ground-breaking results' in the conclusion, and the 26%/16% relative improvement claims in Sec 4.4/4.5 are computed on already high baselines and could be presented more carefully with absolute deltas for clarity.
The paper lacks detail on hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., choice of α in D-FPS, K in EF-KNN, filter dimensionality V) and how these were tuned per-dataset, which affects reproducibility.

Ablation in Table 8 only compares against LSTM as an alternative temporal module; a direct comparison against attention/Transformer-based temporal aggregation (mentioned as a baseline design choice in the text) is not shown quantitively, weakening the argument that Temporal-FA is superior to attention specifically.

The paper does not report FLOPs/latency trade-offs for training (only inference throughput and MACs), nor wall-clock training time, which matters for practical adoption alongside the emphasized efficiency claims.

Limitations section is essentially absent; the paper does not discuss failure cases, applicability of Event Cloud to very high-event-rate scenes where downsampling to fixed T may lose information, or robustness to noise in the raw event stream.

Writing has minor grammatical issues and some formula/notation inconsistencies (e.g., dimension of F vs FC in Eq. 4, T/2 in various equations) that could confuse reproduction efforts without careful cross-referencing to Figure 3.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across ten datasets and three distinct tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is unusually broad for this sub-field and supports claims of general applicability.

The core idea of embracing Event Cloud representation with structural (rather than only input-level) integration of polarity is a reasonable and seemingly novel architectural choice, with the redesigned Grouping & Sampling module (D-FPS, EF-KNN, CES) clearly described.

The frequency-domain Spatial-FA and Temporal-FA modules are well motivated as a way to reduce MACs relative to MLP/conv baselines and to capture long-range temporal dependencies without RNN/attention overhead; complexity analysis (O(D log D) vs O(D^2)) and empirical MACs/parameter comparisons back this up.

Thorough ablation studies (module removal, polarity input-level vs structural-level, Spatial-FA vs convolution replacement, event-number scalability comparison against PointNet++/TTPOINT) give reasonable evidence for the necessity of each component.
Additional FPGA hardware benchmarking (Section 4.7) is a nice touch that goes beyond typical GMACs reporting and strengthens the claimed edge-deployability of the method.
Extensive appendix material (preprocessing time comparison, dimension variance, lookup tables, pseudo-code, visualizations) supports understanding and partial reproducibility of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Improvements over SOTA are inconsistent and sometimes marginal or negative: on N-CARS, SECNet (0.947) is outperformed by EDGCN (0.958) and EV-VGCN/VMST-Net are close; on CIFAR10-DVS and N-Caltech101 gains over VMST-Net are small (<1%). This undercuts the strong rhetorical claims ("ground-breaking results", "far outperforms") used in the text, e.g., for UCF101-DVS the 16% relative gain claim compares against an older SOTA (VMST-Net) rather than the stronger EventMamba baseline shown in the same table, which SECNet only modestly beats (0.967 vs 0.962).

No code is currently available (placeholder link), and while many hyperparameters are given, full reproducibility (exact training scripts, data splits for non-official-split datasets, random seeds) is not guaranteed; no reported variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are given for any experiment, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are statistically meaningful given they are often <1-2 points.

The technical novelty of the frequency-domain component is somewhat incremental, largely adapting existing ideas (GFNet-style global filters, FFC) to a new data modality; the core contribution is more an engineering integration than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea, which is acceptable but should be framed more modestly.

Some notational and organizational issues reduce clarity: overloaded symbols (F used for both feature dimension and feature tensor), Eq. (6)-(7) ordering is confusing (F0 defined after being used in the loop), and Table 13 in the appendix appears to have a formatting/alignment error where DHP19 metric shows two values in one cell inconsistent with other columns.

The justification for feature-based KNN (EF-KNN) over coordinate-based KNN is asserted but not deeply analyzed theoretically or ablated against alternative distance metrics beyond the single reported ablation row, leaving the design choice under-explored.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations in depth (e.g., when Event Cloud's fixed downsampling might discard critical events, sensitivity to the choice of downsampling number T0 across highly variable-density scenes), and the ethics/impact statement is fairly generic.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across ten datasets and three distinct tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), which is unusually broad for a single representation-based backbone paper.

The core architectural idea of embedding polarity into the structural decisions of the Group & Sampling module (rather than only as an input channel) is a reasonable and somewhat novel design choice that is validated through the 'Input P' vs 'w/o P' ablation.

The use of frequency-domain (FFT-based Hadamard product) feature extraction for both spatial (intra-group) and temporal (inter-event) relationships is a sensible way to reduce MACs while retaining global receptive fields, and the complexity argument (O(D log D) vs O(D^2)) is clearly derived.

Efficiency claims are backed by concrete MAC counts, FPS throughput, and even a dedicated FPGA experiment (Section 4.7/Table 10) comparing FFT-based SFA against a spatial MLP baseline, which is a nice extra piece of evidence for hardware deployability.

The ablation studies (module ablation in Table 8, event-number scalability in Table 9, Spatial-FA vs convolution replacement in Appendix I) are reasonably thorough and help isolate contributions of individual components.
weaknesses: Many of the reported gains over the strongest baselines are marginal (e.g., average object-classification accuracy 0.905 vs VMST-Net's 0.902; ASL-DVS 0.9993 vs 0.998; N-CARS SECNet actually underperforms EDGCN 0.958 and MVF-Net 0.968), yet the paper repeatedly uses strong language such as 'ground-breaking results' and 'substantially' which is not well supported by the observed margins, especially without confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics.

No standard deviations, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported anywhere despite comparing methods that differ by hundredths or thousandths of a point on some datasets (e.g., 0.9993 vs 0.998), making it impossible to judge whether reported improvements are meaningful or within noise.

The novelty is largely a recombination of existing techniques (D-FPS from PointNet++, feature-based/EF-KNN similar to DGCNN's dynamic graph construction, global frequency filters from GFNet/FFC) applied to a new data modality; while the combination and application to Event Cloud is reasonable, the individual technical components are not new, and the paper does not always clearly delineate what is genuinely novel versus adapted.

Baselines' reported numbers appear to be taken from prior papers rather than uniformly re-evaluated under the authors' own experimental protocol; combined with the authors' custom 80/20 splits for datasets lacking official partitions, this raises concerns about whether comparisons across methods are conducted on strictly identical splits/pipelines, undermining the reliability of head-to-head comparisons.

There is an unresolved conceptual tension: the paper argues Event Cloud preserves 'fine-grained temporal information' better than voxel/frame representations, yet it still performs fixed random downsampling to a small number of points (1024–10240) regardless of the original (often much larger) event stream length, which could discard substantial temporal detail for long, high-resolution sequences; this trade-off is not analyzed.

Extensive per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (different centroid counts, K, embedding dims across ten datasets, as detailed in the appendix) raises the possibility of overfitting to each benchmark's idiosyncrasies, which weakens claims of general scalability across diverse settings.

The manuscript's presentation is dense and occasionally hard to follow: notation is heavily overloaded across many subscripted symbols (F, G, EC, etc.), several sentences are awkwardly phrased, and key architectural details (e.g., exact per-stage dimension flow) are relegated to the appendix rather than clearly explained in the main text.

Code is stated as 'will be available' with no repository link at submission time, and while extensive hyperparameters are listed in the appendix, full reproducibility (e.g., exact training scripts, per-dataset splits, FPGA implementation details/quantization settings) cannot be verified from the submission alone.

The FPGA benchmark (Table 10) only isolates the Spatial-FA vs. MLP sub-module rather than benchmarking the full SECNet pipeline end-to-end on the FPGA, limiting the practical significance of the hardware-efficiency claim for real deployment scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: existing Point Cloud methods for event data ignore polarity or treat it as an extra input channel and scale poorly to large numbers of events; the paper offers a coherent, reasoned response with an Event Cloud representation plus a structurally polarity-aware Grouping & Sampling (D-FPS + EF-KNN + CES) design.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 10 datasets spanning three distinct tasks (object classification, action recognition, human pose estimation), with numerous baselines from frame-, voxel-, and point-based families, plus preprocessing-time comparisons (Table 4) that are often omitted in prior event-representation papers.

Efficiency claims are backed by multiple types of evidence beyond simple GMAC counts: a lookup table over event-number/centroid configurations (Table 12), FPS/throughput numbers, and a measured FPGA implementation (Table 10) comparing FFT-based Spatial-FA against an MLP baseline, which is a meaningful step toward substantiating real hardware deployability rather than only theoretical complexity.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual components (α scaling, EF-KNN, SFA, TFA, polarity handling) and an explicit ablation replacing the frequency module with convolution (ECNet) to probe the efficiency-accuracy trade-off.

Good supplementary material: dimension-tracing figures, pseudocode, and a qualitative comparison table (Table 11) situating the architecture relative to prior representations/methods, aiding reproducibility and understanding of design choices.
weaknesses: The appendix ablation (Table 13, Section I) shows that replacing Spatial-FA with a standard convolution (ECNet) generally yields *better* accuracy than SECNet across most datasets, sometimes by a non-trivial margin (e.g., DHP19 MPJPE 69.89 vs 66.87, UCF101-DVS 0.916 vs 0.941, N-CARS 0.947 vs 0.951). This means the central 'frequency-aware module' claim in the main text primarily buys efficiency at a real accuracy cost, but this trade-off is not clearly acknowledged in the main paper's narrative, which instead states the frequency module 'does not give too much of a discount' on performance — this is an overstatement given the appendix's own data.

Main-table results are mixed rather than uniformly state-of-the-art: on object classification (Table 2), SECNet trails EDGCN on N-CARS (0.947 vs 0.958) and VMST-Net on N-Caltech101 (0.824 vs 0.822 is close but not a clear win), undermining the framing in the abstract/intro of clear, consistent superiority over voxel-based SOTA.

Several datasets (N-Caltech101, CIFAR10-DVS, ASL-DVS, Daily DVS, UCF101-DVS) lack official train/test splits and the paper uses a self-selected random 20% split; it is unclear whether the numbers reported for baseline methods (often taken from their original papers) used the same split, raising a fairness/comparability concern for these result tables.

No code release at submission time (placeholder link), and while an algorithm/pseudocode is given, several implementation-critical details (e.g., exact learnable filter V dimensionality and initialization for Spatial-FA vs Temporal-FA, treatment of complex-valued FFT outputs before the nonlinearity) are not fully specified in the main text, which could hinder exact reproducibility.

No reported variance/multiple runs or confidence intervals for any of the results; given several performance differences versus baselines are small (e.g., <1 point in several classification tables), the lack of statistical treatment weakens the strength of comparative claims.

The novelty of using FFT/Hadamard-product frequency modules for feature extraction is incremental relative to existing frequency-domain vision literature (FFC, GFNet, SpectFormer) already surveyed in Section 2.2; the core innovation is adapting these ideas to 1D event-cloud sequences, which is a reasonable but modest algorithmic contribution rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Some presentation issues: the conclusion's use of the term 'ground-breaking results' is unsupported, hyperbolic language; notation is dense (Fi, FGi, FSi, FAi, FTi, FRi, etc.) and cross-referencing between the main paper and extensive appendix (spread across 10+ heavily lettered sections) makes the paper harder to follow in a single pass.
